ColonyCouncil.WhatsNewPageDef.label: what's new
ColonyCouncil.WhatsNewPageDef.summary: What changed in each update of Rimfolk, newest first.
ColonyCouncil.WhatsNewPageDef.description:
Rimfolk is updated often. Each update is listed here with its highlights, newest first, so you can see what is new since you last played. The same list is in CHANGELOG.md, beside the mod's files in the downloaded or cloned folder.
When you load a save after an update, a letter lists the newest round once. The setting "A letter after each update" (Interface page of the mod settings) turns it off.

points.li: A new couple is noticed: both write of it, and those closest to them say they're glad, or, for family who can't stand the one chosen, that they have their doubts. An engagement gets the parents' blessing.
A proposal turned down sends the one who asked on a long walk alone, and later their closest friend finds them and says the right thing.
When a pregnancy begins to show, the mother tells her partner, glad or worried, and each tells their own parents, the grandparents to be. Expecting parents can wish for a crib.
A child lost before birth is grieved by the grandparents too. The parents get the rest of the day to themselves, and someone close goes to sit with the mother.
Naming a baby offers the family's own first names, and the story says who a colonist was named after. Growth birthdays and coming of age end with a family toast at the table that evening.

A carving, a stool, a knife or a book an answer says someone made is made first: its maker works at the colony's bench for it (or at the camp's fire, or at the table) for an hour or two, with the game's working effect, and only then carries it over. Before, it appeared at once.

Wood a guest, the hired hands or the camp's people cut comes from trees they really go and fell, one after another with the game's own cutting. The logs are left for the colony, and the answer's words are told once the trees are down.
The children's trees, and a tree planted in someone's memory, are planted by hand: each walks out to their own spot and digs it in, and the sapling is in the ground when they're done.
A new room is staked out when the walk out to the ground gets there, not when the answer is given.

A fallen star is forged into a blade at the colony's smithy, or broken up where it fell by someone sent out to it. A crashed drone is stripped or its memory pulled at the wreck. The wild bees' comb is cut from a real tree near the fields, and the lightning-struck tree is felled by hand.

li.title: As the answer said, in its own time

points.li: A feast an answer spends raw food on is cooked first. In the hours before it, its organizer (or the colony's best cook among those asked) cooks that food into meals at one of the colony's stoves, the best meal they can make there, and the feast waits while the pot is on. The food is no longer taken from the stores when the answer is given, so the colony doesn't pay twice.
A fight or a walk-out that an answer's risk brings comes partway into the supper, work party or visit the answer set going, where its words put it, instead of the moment the answer is given.
An errand carries all of what it was given: the carrier goes back to the stores for more loads instead of the rest vanishing, and goods for the camp are handed to someone of the camp.
A visit or a lesson the colony was told of that never came about now says so and why, instead of passing without a word. A visit cut short no longer reports its outcome as if it had happened.

A colonist's story shows their family tree: partner, parents, brothers and sisters, children, grandparents and grandchildren, step-family and in-laws, with their age and where each is now (here, away, with another people, a prisoner, buried here...).
Family by marriage counts: a spouse's parents, a child's spouse, a step-parent or step-child are worried about, felt as family at home, grieved when they die, and can come to visit.
When someone joins the colony and family of theirs already lives here, the relative goes to find them: a reunion, with a word, a moment of joy for both and a memory they share.

A colonist who sees family among the raiders says so, and the colony hears of it. If that relative is taken prisoner, the council is asked whether to let them go home, let the colonist try to talk them round, or keep them like any other prisoner.

li.title: The enemy dead, as the council said

points.li: A new answer for the enemy dead when the colony has a crematorium working: "Into the crematorium". The bodies are carried in one at a time and burned there the same day, their gear left beside it.

"Burn them" carries the dead out late in the afternoon. At dusk one of those who carried them takes wood from the stores out to the pyre and lights it, and the bodies lie burning on it through the night instead of vanishing under a campfire; by morning they are ash where they lay.

"Give them graves" and "One grave for all of them" dig real graves outside the wall, a grave each or side by side as one trench, and the raiders are laid in them, instead of being hauled wherever the colony keeps its dead. The graves take strangers only.
The words of these answers say only what happens on the map: no scavengers heard at dusk, no lamp oil or markers nobody put there.
The People roster shows beside a colonist's age how many years they spent in cryptosleep, from two years on.

A colonist's story has a new part, Across the years: when they were born, how many of the years since they lived, and each parent, grandparent, child or grandchild whose age runs the wrong way round (a mother younger than her son, a grandson older than his grandmother), with whose years asleep explain it.
Now and then, when two such relatives are together, one says a word about it to the other, in their own voice.

With Hospitality, a guest with enough friends to join could keep a grey Recruit button ("This guest can not be recruited (right now)") after a save was loaded in the same session: Hospitality went on reading the guest from the save loaded before. Rimfolk now clears Hospitality's guest records as each game loads, so the button, the guest areas and the guest tab's ticks belong to the guest in front of you.
"Burn them" for the enemy dead tells how it went once the pyre has burned down at dawn, not while the bodies are being carried out hours before it is lit.
A pyre that can't be lit for two days, with danger every evening, no longer leaves the bodies forbidden beside the gate: they are let go for the colony to see to.

With RimMarket, a colony stall's "Set up the stall" opens Rimfolk's own sales table. On the left the colony's goods by category, with a search and a sort by worth, count or name; a click puts all of an article on the counter, a right-click asks how many.

On the right only what is for sale, a card a line: how many, the quality range, the price on a slider with what it fetches each and for the whole line, how well it sells at that price, and what has sold and lies on the counter.
One price for every line at once (a bargain, the usual, dear), and at the foot what it all comes to and how often shoppers come at these prices.
It changes only RimMarket's own sale lines, so RimMarket's window still works on the same stall; switch back to it with "RimMarket's sales table, Rimfolk's way" on the Interface page.

Fixed a bug in the game itself: when one build needed more of a material than the colony had, builders could stop carrying that material to every other build too: a research bench short of steel could keep a drug lab from ever being started, while the builders mined or tended animals. Each build is now judged on its own.

A build still waits until all of a material it still needs is on the map before anyone carries any of it, as the game has it. A bench that needs more steel than there is waits for it, and its frame's inspect pane shows what's missing.
The Defenses page has its own "defense" button in the bottom bar, right after the council's, and opens in a window of its own. The same page stays in the council's Colony section.

A click on a raid's warning on the panels, the Defenses page key, and coming back from picking a line's spot now open that window. The button can be hidden on the settings' Interface page, like the rooms button.

A decree the colony needs now and wants can come again sooner: after fight on fight, with the home filthy and many hurt, a clean sweep someone asks for is possible again in about four days instead of eight.
A needed repeat is minded less: those against it lose less trust, resent it less while it lasts, and are less likely to snap.
It never becomes a decree for every day: at least a day and a third of its rest always stays, and once it has been declared twice in a month the need counts for half.
The decree's card says when it's needed and why, and how much the colony wants it. A clean sweep and a sick bay also count the fighting as a need.

The game still chooses each weather from the land's own, Seasonal Weather's and other mods' included, but Rimfolk weighs the choice by the land and the last days. Spells of rain and of dry weather hold and then break, a long dry spell in the warm with a storm.

One weather follows another as it would: a storm seldom comes out of a clear sky except on a hot afternoon, fog comes after a cold clear night or rain, and a cold front brings snow, or a storm where it's still warm. A morning fog lifts by late morning.

Each land keeps its character. A desert's dry spells run longer and its wet ones end sooner, a tropical land Seasonal Weather doesn't cover gets a wet and a dry season, and over the years every land keeps about the rain it had. Special weathers and anything an event forces are left alone.

Rimfolk's events move the weather after them: the long rains bring more rain, a thirsty herd comes in a dry spell that holds, and the sky clears after hail. Heat waves, warm spells and cold snaps bring clear skies, and no drought ever brings more rain.
The weather moves the temperature a few degrees: cooler under rain on a warm day, colder on clear nights (much colder in the desert), milder under cloud.

The colonist who reads the weather best says what's coming a few hours ahead, and the Overview's Weather card shows it. The weather that comes is held to, and the forecast is as good as the one who makes it; a weather station from Stormproof or Weather Control makes it nearly certain.
Each year leans a little wetter or drier, warmer or colder, and the annals say so when it was. Each part has its own setting under "The weather" on the Events page.

Each home map keeps a weather record. The coldest night, the hottest day, the longest rain and the longest dry spell since the colony came are remarked on when broken, and the first snow is set against last year's. The Overview page has a Weather card.
Each season is set against the same season a year before, and one far from usual here is remembered by a name ("the winter of the long cold", "the dry summer") in the chronicle and the year's annals.
Rimfolk's events that speak of the weather only come after it: the long rains after rain on four of the last seven days, an ice fair after five frozen days, a struck tree after a storm, and six more.

Hail is seen coming: two hours of green sky, a word from the one who knows the fields best, and a few colonists bringing in the ripe crops. Fixed: hail no longer brings rain below freezing, and its rain no longer runs on for a day or two after it.

Three quirks: loves the snow, follows the sun, sleeps best in rain, two of them with a free-time habit of their own. Breath shows on bitter mornings, steam rises off outdoor fires and the sauna's door in the cold, and one who dreads storms flinches at lightning.
A storm keeps a trade caravan half a day longer, and snowbound land slows the people coming for a mission.

With Seasonal Weather: firebreak advice on a dry, windy day in the fire season, with a button that marks the brush round the home area for cutting, and a work party round the roofs and walls after an earthquake.
Stormproof, Weather is kinda cozy, SS Lightning Rod, Disasters: Tornado and Quiet Wonders are met where they're installed, and all are safe to add to a running save.

Hold Ctrl and right-drag with drafted colonists to send them to cover. The cell you press is where they gather and the drag points at the enemy; each one takes the cell nearby with the most cover from that side that they can shoot from.
Long guns stand a step back and melee fighters a step forward, two cells apart where there is room, in the order they stood. Each cell's cover shows while you drag: green from 50%, yellow from 20%.

Ctrl and a right-click without dragging takes cover from the nearest enemies in sight. Nobody is sent off the edge of the map, and a right-click on something with its own orders is the game's as before.

It runs on the game's own drag of several colonists, so it works in 1.7, where the TakeCover mod shows the colonists where they would go but never gives the order. With Rimfolk's on, TakeCover can be removed. A setting, on the Interface page.

Time together no longer makes everyone friends. How two colonists get on follows the game's own compatibility between them: a deep talk or chitchat between two who don't click counts for a third to two thirds as much, and a slight or a quarrel stings a little more.

After a few days side by side the way two get on shows in the Social tab: they don't click, rub each other the wrong way or get on each other's nerves (3 to 10 points, deepening over a month), or they are easy company or on the same wavelength. Partners are left alone.
Rimfolk's warm moments come up less often between two who don't click, and frictions more; the other way round for two who get on easily.

Fighting side by side is respect rather than friendship: comrades add 3, 5 or 8 points instead of 4, 8 or 14. Before, a colony that drafted everyone for each raid had every pair 14 points closer to friends.

Defense plans are drawn for your colony: from its shooters and how far their weapons reach, whether the raiders it meets throw grenades, its bows, how big raids are and the turret it would build. The planner says what each was drawn for, and Shooters and Depth add or take away.

Killboxes laid out by what the 1.6 game code shows: the way in turns twice, then runs straight for four or five cells, so a raider at the last corner can't see your shooters; every shooter stands within about 24° of the doorway's line, where its walls give the raider in it no cover, and against grenades more than a throw back. Decoy mini-turrets in the box, or an autocannon behind the gap in the line; traps and things that slow them in the way in, never in the box.

Firing positions in pockets: a piece of wall in front and sandbags at its corners and beside it, for three-quarters cover while leaning out to shoot. The killbox, the firing line and the sniper's post use them, and a line's review counts them.
A baffled gate: a passage that turns into a walled yard, a small killbox that is also the colony's way in. Against raiders who throw grenades, a line's first step offers it where it fits.

Side lines behind a gate stand where nobody outside sees them and the gate gives a raider little cover. The perimeter wall has an airlock, a gate, a cell and a gate; the trap corridor puts a fence beside each trap; turrets in a nest stand beyond each other's blast; the mortar pit keeps its mortars and shells apart.
The palisade and castle gates have a killing yard: archers behind embrasures across its far side, and the way on through a gate in its corner, where the melee fighters wait.
A line's review offers to plan a killbox again when the colony outgrows it, or when it was laid out before plans were drawn and its last corner sees the shooters.

The Almanac's defense pages say what holds in 1.6: raiders take an open way however long it is, stop and shoot from sandbags too and lean round corners; how a pocket works; where shooters stand in a killbox; and how far a turret's blast reaches.

With Ideology, every meal bill but the fungus meal's starts with fungus unticked, so the cooks keep the fungus for fungus meals. Tick it back on any bill that should use it; a dish from another mod that can't be made without fungus keeps it.
In a save from before this, the meal bills already in a queue get fungus unticked once, when the save is loaded.
A lucky charm counts whenever it's on them, worn, in hand, as a sidearm or in their pack, not only while they hold it.

Build priorities: a button on every blueprint and frame sets it low, normal, high or urgent (a click steps through for everything selected, a right-click picks one). Builders leave a level alone while something higher can go ahead, with its materials on the map, reachable and within someone's skill; a job you give by hand is always taken, a blueprint keeps its level as a frame, and a light tint on the map shows the level: red for urgent, amber for high, blue for low. The setting "Build priorities on blueprints" turns it off.

Camps come about once a season, on a timer of their own, instead of once in years. Every kind of camp can be asked something now, and 14 asks are the camp's own requests, walked into the colony by its people: water for the herd, a stall at the gate, prayers at the graves, an apprentice at a sick bed, a test hole. Eight new council questions are about a camp.

Colonists talk about the day coming up on the calendar, the latest world news and the camp on the map, and children get a talk of their own, about growing up here. Talk repeats far less, about 6,900 lines where there were 2,600, every voice with its own lines for each turn, memory and in-joke, and none of it at the wrong moment: no teasing on a day of mourning.

Fourteen new everyday events (a killing frost, something at the pens, fire on the far ridge, a war band in the valley, a gambler, a traveling teacher and more), new turns for nine of the most frequent, and two season-long stories: an apprentice from the town and a traveler with a fever.

Seven new world events (a prophet on the roads, an old vault opened, markets closed between two peoples, a merchant house failing, the ice road in a hard freeze, a moot of the peoples, an old thrumbo and its horn hunters), and eleven older ones play differently a second time, following from what the colony did.

45 new dreams, so nearly every habit, quirk, life goal and story has one, and eight quirks the colony lives into: a lamp lit for travelers, a horror of smoke, coins counted twice, the fields walked at dawn, a dream book, a healer's salve, juggling at supper, a trick against the cold.

Calendar days from what the colony lived through (a camp's gift, a world event it took part in, the faith's holy days, one brought home from captivity), kept with a walk out to what the day remembers; memories and deeds from camps, missions and world events, and jokes passed on to a friend who missed them; ten bad days that follow from what happened, like rain on a feast day; and 22 encounters by the water and under rare skies.

The gate, the perimeter wall and the sandbag line put a piece of wall at the outer end of each sandbag line, so a raider who swings wide can't shoot along it, and a new wall and sandbag firing line, for where raiders come straight on, gives each of six shooters a wall on either side.

A colonist carried off by raiders no longer counts against anyone: their wish is let go quietly instead of running out against the council and those who backed it, their birthday and anniversaries stay on the calendar, and their hours come back after a rest day.
An answer never turns a people hostile on its own: a loss of goodwill stops at -60, as the world events' always did.
A wish or goal to tame a new animal counts real tamings (and catches), not a chick hatched or a dog bought, and a hunt wish isn't met by slaughtering in the pens.
A curfew declared on a rest day gives the evening hours back to what they were before the rest day, not to recreation for good.

A mission stays on the home it was taken on at; Rimfolk's events, visitors and couriers keep to homes on the ground, never an orbital base; an escort starts only with a caravan setting out from the colony itself.

A sleepwalker's door is bolted only while it's still their own room's, and only for the nights asked; a talent scout's offer can't be taken once the colonist is gone; and what a story waits for two people to share now survives a save and load.

The people world news sends to the gate now come: a feud's runaway and the elder who takes the blood price, the toll-keeper's man, a smith and a merchant's agent who buy and pay on the spot, pilgrims and prospectors camping by the water, a deserter, two claimants' riders.

Small sums and food change hands on the map too: visitors count out their tips, a beaten challenger hands over the stake, a neighbor's runner pays for a find the colony sells, the lord's carters come for a tithe in kind, and food for the hungry who keep coming is carried out to them at the gate.

Camps look the part: a salt caravan's pack beasts and porters, the drovers' herd grazing beyond the camp with a dog at the leader's heels, hunters dressing their kills at camp, the refugees' washing by the windbreak, the hermit's woodpile.

Camps leave as they lived: healers look in on the colony's sick before going, mourners plant a sprig by the door, the hermit leaves a carved bird, players their painted backdrop, tree-singers a ring of saplings, and a traveling smith may mend a damaged door or wall for nothing.

Council choices you see happen: lantern night lights real torches until dawn, the enemy dead are carried out to a pyre that burns through the night or to the tree line, a cold elder gets a fire or a warmer room, a sleepwalker's door is bolted at night, a doctor goes round to everyone, and the night watch walks the walls.

Gifts by hand: a carving, a replacement keepsake, an old debt's gift and an old crafter's knife are carried over and set at the other's feet, and the moods wait for it; the scribe's copy is a real book, and a coffin stands in its owner's room.
Story endings you can see: a secret told is said to the gathered colony, a recurring dream ends with a long look at what was made, and a companion animal keeps at its person's heels for a day or two.

The architect menu's build buttons can be clicked again where an on-screen panel lies behind them: the panel steps aside under the buttons and the info box, as it already did under the colonist bar and the inspect pane.

Five habits of the quieter work: reading at every meal (research, a little faster), knowing every prisoner by name (warden work, a little more persuasive), mending their own clothes (tailoring: the worst-worn thing they wear mends a little each day), doodling in the margins (art: now and then inspired at it) and sleeping light (after fighting fires: they wake when fire breaks out near them). Each has a word of its own on the map.
Two more traits of Rimfolk's own grow out of them: a scholar from months of reading at meals, a mender from months of mending.

Habits pass between people who spend their days together: a child picks one up from a parent, a student from their mentor, lovers, family and good friends from each other, the closer the sooner. The habit's line says whom they had it from; fears, grief and lucky things never pass.

li.title: Plans that hold, guests who go

points.li: Hovering a trap plan near the top or bottom of the map no longer throws an error every frame.

A cooler that can't go into a room's wall (something of yours in the way, or the ground) no longer leaves a hole there: the wall goes up in its place, and with "replace your own" on, what stands there is taken down for it like on the rest of the wall.
A defense piece that lies partly in unexplored ground has the rock in its visible part mined too, and the build queue waits until all of it has come to light before giving up on it.
A raid's lessons count raiders who arrive late or are seen again after loading a save, and removing a line during a raid no longer credits raiders to the wrong line.
A visit or lesson never calls a colonist away from a meal, their bed, a rescue or another plan, nor anyone urgently hungry or very tired, and it ends once they need to eat or sleep.
When you arrest one of a group of visitors, the rest leave at once instead of standing at the gate for a day; visitors walled in on their way out leave after a day.
A camp no longer stops hunting or felling trees for a day or more after you load an earlier save or another colony.

A courier who never reached the colony gives up a day after setting out, not a day after you sent for them, and a trip whose courier was captured, enslaved or stuck at the edge now ends instead of waiting forever.
A courier's pack animal leaves with them when the courier goes, instead of staying behind on the map.
A courier whose drop spot was walled off or built over leaves the goods where they stand rather than trying to reach it.
Loading another save no longer shows the last game's alerts, wounds or idle times in the on-screen panels, and the inventory's yesterday column now works with up to eight home maps.
The hover card lets go of a colonist who died or left the map while the mouse rested on it, and a panel's options window redraws the panel when you reset it.

A colonist who took up another ideoligion could flip back to the old one within days and back again, losing their role each time. Now they settle into it for a year, during which no leaning wears on them or takes over; the one they left stays only a small leaning, and a fading leaning never takes over. Someone with dear friends on both sides may still change in a long while, never back and forth.
An ideoligion the game has let go of, its last believers gone, is forgotten: nobody leans toward it, shows it on the Culture tab or takes it up.

A visiting scholar who speaks at a gathering is no longer woken, called away from a meal or a sickbed, or walked out of a cell to the table. Choosing what to work on costs a little less while a clean sweep isn't on.
Remembering every birthday could never take root or grow into kindness: it's lived only on someone's birthday, and asked for sixty. Four birthdays remembered now do it.

Knocking on wood gladdened colonists wounded early in a long fight: now only those with no wound since the fight began. That mood and the best bite's follow the setting for moods, like every other, and with quirks switched off, nobody's hidden habits live on, take root or make news.
A deep-rooted habit now lasts four months after they stop, as its line says, and one habit leads to one trait change: humming that steadies the lazy is spent on it.

Wishes talk about what they are: a fountain, a sculpture or flowers about making the colony beautiful, a guest bed or a comms console about guests and neighbours, recruiting or freeing a prisoner about the prisoner, a council meeting about the council. A promised wish that lapses says its own words for the broken promise first, and a first anniversary's "it still feels new here" can come at last.

li.title: Habits that grow from a life

points.li: Each quirk on a colonist's Story tab, under Heart, now says how it came, what it does and how long it lasts: "can't stand a mess (from all the cleaning). Cleaning speed +10%, mood -2 in a messy room, tidies up in their free time. Stays while they keep at cleaning." One that does nothing to play says so.

Habits come each in their own way. Most grow out of what someone does: Rimfolk notes once an hour what each colonist is doing (their kind of work, early mornings, late nights, time outdoors) and remembers about three weeks of it. A habit of work never comes without its work, and the more of it, the likelier. A few are simply who someone is and come to anyone they fit.

Seven new habits: steady hands (doctoring), measures twice (building), sharpens every blade (smithing), knows every trail (hunting), carries more than they should (hauling), keeps late hours (being up after eleven), and can't sit still (by nature).
A habit lived doesn't fade while it is. Lived on sixty days, it takes root and its knack and good mood grow a little (cleaning 15% faster instead of 10%, say).

Every habit shows on the map: a moment of its own in their free time (tidying a dirty room, watching the sun come up, looking for pretty stones, looking in on the sick, wishing someone a happy birthday) or a word now and then at the work.

The superstitions that were only flavour do something small: knocking on wood gladdens after a fight come through unhurt, talking to the dead comforts near the graves, counting everything warns when the food won't last the week, salting the doorway keeps nightmares away, and a sleep talker's roommate sleeps a little worse (a lover finds it endearing).

A habit lived for months grows into a trait: harder work, kindness, night owl, or one of six traits of Rimfolk's own that are only ever earned (tidy, green thumb, born cook, animal friend, healer's hands, trail-wise). With Vanilla Traits Expanded, its neat and animal lover are given instead. Tough and fast walker can now be earned too, never lost.
The character page shows "where life is taking them": the trait changes a colonist is heading toward, with how many of the things that lead there have happened. Hover one for the list.

The gate with sandbag lines put its sandbags three cells straight behind the gate, which a defense line's own review calls too close: the first raider through was on the shooters at once, and raiders outside could see the nearest of them through the gap. Its sandbags now stand five cells back and off to either side of the way through, like the sandbag line's, with three firing positions behind each.

The perimeter wall's sandbags moved the same way, five cells back from its inner gate. A plan that closes a gap can no longer bring cover closer than a line's review allows, and the advice for a gate with too little cover says how far back to put it.

Each colonist now leans toward the other ideoligions around them, shown as bars under their certainty on the Culture tab, growing, fading or holding. Believers they like, love or are family to pull hardest, and a leaning fades when nothing feeds it.

The strongest leaning wears on their certainty against the game's own daily recovery. When it passes their certainty, they take that ideoligion up through the game's own conversion, and the one they leave becomes a leaning they may drift back to. A leaning passing half is told once.

The one-ideoligion decree now draws everyone of another ideoligion, not only the wavering, who were almost never there because content colonists stay at full certainty. With friends among its believers, a content colonist comes round in about a month; a lone believer of a minority never pulls the rest over.
Talks, evenings, crises and council answers that sway someone toward an ideoligion feed their leaning toward it as well.

The game's messages at the top left are drawn over the on-screen panels, and were hard to read over a panel's own lines. A message that touches a panel now sits in a box of its own (a dark fill with a thin light edge, behind the whole line), fading with the message; over the open map it looks as it always did.
A decree used lately says on its card in how many days it's safe to enact again, and "used once" or "used 3 times" instead of "1 time(s)".

Everything colonists say over their heads was reread one line at a time: council talk, wish asks and reminders, everyday talk, gossip, visitors' lines and group talk. Each makes its point in its first sentence, and a speech bubble now shows the whole line when it fits instead of only its first sentence.

The social log reads like the game's own. Moments, frictions, conversations and small social events are one sentence about what was said, at any hour and wherever the two stand. Nobody tidies a grave, fetches a meal or walks the walls when the game shows no such thing, and a friendly contest's opening line no longer gives away a different result from the winner's.

Conversations hang together: replies answer whatever was said, closing lines fit either side, and wish talk fits every wish it serves (health and healing, the lost and the dead, animals, safety, what children need).

Calendar letters, eulogies, the annals, group journals, personality marks, trait changes and quirks are written for the moment they come: no grave before a burial, no rite claimed that wasn't held, no children, pens or walls the colony may not have, and no sentence opening on a lower-case name.
A beast or pet nobody named is "the warg", not "warg", and talk about a disaster says "the cold snap" instead of "Cold snap" in the middle of a sentence.

Only a joyful ritual (a feast, a dance, a festival) is talked about afterwards as a party; an execution or a sacrifice no longer is. A Pokémon's evolution is congratulated aloud instead of turning up as a quote with no speaker in the log.
Moods from small social events hold for every event that gives them ("made fun of", "made to feel small"), and British spellings that had slipped in are American now.

Words said to a gathering (a lesson, a story, an apology, a letter read out) are no longer a party where everyone wanders about. The speaker stands at the head of the table, the listeners sit in the chairs round it facing them, and the rest stand close by; with no table near, they stand in a ring round the speaker.

A visiting scholar who is asked to teach now comes to the table and gives the lesson there, instead of walking about while the colony follows, and the lesson is held at the dining table when there is one.

What a lesson teaches goes to those who sat through it, when it's over, and the closing message says who learned what ("Hector, Harper and 3 others learned from it: intellectual +800 xp each"). The scholar's lesson teaches 800 xp instead of 350, since it no longer goes to everyone.
During a clean sweep, everyone who can clean does it before their other work, even those not set to clean, until the home area is clean. The decree's card says so.

Fires, the sick and wounded, children, prisoners and cooking still come before the scrubbing, and so do sleep, meals and washing. It's one of the deeper game hooks: with them off, the work order is your own.

Colonists still healing from a wound or an illness now like a clean sweep (unless they're lazy) and resting when ill (unless they're industrious or tough), and the Decrees page shows them among those who like it.

When many are hurt (two colonists or more, and at least a third of the colony, with real wounds still healing, not a scratch), colonists petition the council for either decree. Before, resting when ill was only asked for when someone was ill, and a clean sweep only when the colony was dirty.

Every dream was reread and many retold: some are a bare image, some a half-memory or a feeling that stays into the morning, fewer start with "I dreamt" or end with waking up, and a dream of a raid or an evolution never reads as if it really happened.

Every journal line was reread on its own. Entries are shorter and uneven, in each colonist's own voice, and true to the moment they're written: no funeral before anyone is buried, a blessing told by the one who received it, no snow promised in a dry winter.

Journal entries go by the hour the moment happened (a loss, a fight, an arrival, an everyday thing), so night and morning lines show when they should, instead of always or never depending on where the colony lies.

Comrades from a fight who drift apart now each write a line about it; before, nothing was written at all. Two lines about kept promises now show, and the yearly day of a fight where an old enemy came back is remembered as such.
When a nemesis dies to a trap, a turret or an illness, the one they hurt no longer writes about thanking themselves for it.
The dates on this page are corrected: rounds from 0.8.0 on had drifted up to a week ahead of when they came out.

What colonists plan on their own (a light or a bed for themselves, a personal touch in their room, a floor, a grave, the thing a wish of theirs asks for) is only ever of plain materials: wood, stone blocks or bone. They no longer spend the colony's steel, silver, gold, plasteel, cloth or components; something that needs those isn't planned at all.
What the council plans for a promised wish is made of wood or stone blocks too when it can be, and of the colony's finer materials only when nothing plainer will do.

About 1,600 moods were reread one at a time. Each now says what happened in this colony with one concrete thing from the moment ("I still get up at feeding time"), and holds for every answer, variant or risk that gives it, including half-hearted customs and verdicts the council reuses.

Moods no longer claim what the game didn't do: a sold animal leaves with its buyer instead of running loose, a reburied grave doesn't moralize, and a story's mood fits however the story went. About 35 mood names were clarified or shortened to fit the mood list.
The "what helps" tips were checked against the game's own numbers (how long things last, who is spared, what really helps) and use the interface's own names.

li.title: A health panel at a glance

points.li: The health panel speaks the Health tab's language: each condition carries the game's own icon (tended well, tended poorly, needs tending, the blood drop), a tiny bar for how far a wound has healed or how an illness's immunity race stands, and its tending in red, yellow or green.

Conditions are small chips that wrap onto a second line instead of being cut off ("Bruise ×2", then "+N"), each with its own tooltip. Each colonist gets a small health bar by the name, a coloured word (healing green, getting worse orange, bleeding red) and their pain on hover. "Icons and bars" in the panel's options gives the plain look back.

li.title: Panels that stay on the screen

points.li: A panel taller than the screen (the inventory with every row shown) now stops at the game's button bar and scrolls: the mouse wheel over it, or the thin bar at its right edge, which you can drag or click above and below. The inventory's search box scrolls with it.
The panels' options show all of their settings again. The inventory's were cut off after its first look, so its rows, order, pins and the rest couldn't be set.

The inspect tabs over the colonist's pane (Story, Mood, Gear and the rest) take your clicks again where a panel lies behind them, also when another mod such as RimHUD draws them wider or from the left edge.

Picking a spot for a new defense line by hand can now turn the line: the rotate keys (or the game's rotate buttons above the menu) turn which way it faces from the way the helper worked out, and the cursor says which way it faces and how to turn it.
Placing a defense plan by hand ("Place it myself") shows the same rotate buttons beside its keys.

Every wish, life goal, decree and council ambition was reread line by line. Colonists ask in more ways (a hint, a demand, a bargain, a complaint), the cold voice bargains or unsettles instead of reciting costs, and thanks can be a single word.

Wish lines fit every way a wish comes true: thanks are said the moment it's granted, a lapsed wish no longer claims the trouble passed or that the council said no, and a room of one's own fits someone with no bed as well as someone in the barracks.

Life goals read right in a letter ("let go of an old shame", "find faith again"), each line fits whatever set the goal off, and the letter when a goal or an ambition is reached is a plain sentence about who did it and how long it took.
Decree lines hold whether they're said in a petition, when the decree is declared or while it runs, and the curfew's grumbling counts the hours.

The people a world event's letter speaks of are there. The rider waits by the gate until you answer and takes what you send; the family asking for shelter waits with their dog or goat, and the ones you take in are the ones you met. Only people at peace with the colony come, only when it's safe, and they go home if the weather turns on them.

Guests given a night stay it, by the wall or in a corner of the dining room on a bitter night, and go on at first light. Drovers graze their herd on the far meadow overnight, and mourners, a clan's band or a lord's progress pass along the road.

More of what answers only told now happens: a night watch on the walls, a shearing day that shears the herd, a grieving colonist sitting at the grave, the long road told by the fire, a family supper at one table, and visitors shown round, taught from and sung with.

What answers name now exists: the apology carving and a repaid debt's gift are real sculptures signed by their maker, guests who cut wood leave real stumps and logs, the children's trees are saplings in the ground, and a staked-out room appears as building plans.
A visitor's dog only comes up when there is one, the traveling healer only for an old injury, and the animal in decline only when it's old or ill. A few event lines that could never show now can.

Goods that events move between the colony and the world now move on the map. Sell corn to a village and their porters walk in some hours later, go to your stockpile and carry it off; the silver comes back with a runner. A big load brings one of their pack animals. Gifts, payments, rewards and bought goods are carried in and set down by the gate.

Errands to the gate are handed to someone who really waits there. A prisoner you sell is led off by the buyer's riders, a runaway animal by its owners' herder, lost cargo and a crashed drone by their owners, who pay the finder's fee on the spot.

Letters about a venture, a market or a fair now arrive with the goods. Couriers come by day, only when the map is safe, and say a word or two in their own people's way; if nobody can come, or the setting "Goods and people come and go on the map" is off, everything happens at once as before. The Almanac page "goods carried by hand" explains it.

li.title: Every event in its own voice

points.li: About 1,250 events, questions and stories were rewritten one at a time: storyteller events, world situations, council dilemmas, encounters, personal stories, missions, camps and secrets. Each now has the length its moment deserves, from a single line for a passing sight to a full letter for a disaster, and opens its own way.

Where the story gives a reason, people speak for themselves: a burned town's shaky message, a toll-keeper's terms chalked on a board, a plague doctor's printed form passed through the gate, an officer's summons, a hermit's six words, a reeve's hurried letter, a child's petition in charcoal.

Some events now arrive as what they are: the list found under a hoarder's bed, an elder's ledger read out column by column, a funeral plan in a colonist's own hand, a warlord's price, a work song, a playbill nailed by the road.

Outcomes say what happened instead of how everyone felt about it, and stop on an image rather than a moral. Each camp's people sound like themselves: terse hunters, a tired refugee family, cocky prospectors, theatrical players, precise surveyors.
When a personal story ends, its letter reads as one short tale (an opening, a turn, an ending) instead of a list of stages.

About sixty texts that contradicted the game were fixed: outcomes that told of days passing when they show at once, letters that showed an unfilled place name or began a sentence in lowercase, gifts said to be at the gate when they land elsewhere, carts, oxen and goats that never appear, and a default answer that claimed the council had ruled when it never answered.

The health panel's summary line no longer runs words together ("Bruisetended 27%"): each condition and how it stands are spaced apart again, and so are the pieces of the mood line in the Needs tab. Something that can kill but isn't a wound or an illness (a gene's chemical dependency, hypothermia) shows once it's a tenth of the way, not from the first hour, and says "towards deadly".
Click "and 15 more" under any panel to show every row; "Rows before 'and more'" in the panel's options sets the limit again.

Rimfolk now calls the game's belief system what the game does: the ideoligion, and how firmly someone holds it, their certainty. The People page shows "Ideoligions", the setting is "Ideoligions in the colony", the council calls an ideoligion evening or names one the colony's ideoligion, and the colonist bar warns of wavering certainty. It was always the game's own Ideology system, not a religion of Rimfolk's.

Colonists still speak of their faith in their own voice: in what they say, in their journals and in a crisis of faith. The council's buttons on an ideoligion's card take a second row when they don't fit side by side.

li.title: A defense helper that reads your line

points.li: The defense helper knows a pass your line already holds: a gap just in front of it, or the same pass measured further out, now reads "covered by the south-west pass" and is no longer offered as a new line. Your gate, the doors in the line's wall and a door across its gap count as its way through even when shut, so a closed gate never makes it look for another way in; the line's card says to hold the gate open during a raid.

"Plan this step" lays the trap corridor on the raiders' own route to your gate, in front of the line, using the rock for its sides where it can, and says why it chose that spot, or why nothing fits and what would make room.

Before it proposes walls, the helper checks whether they would send raiders another way, and offers to leave the corridor's sides open or to close the other gap first. It reads the map again when you build or take down walls, doors, traps or cover near a line ("Survey again" does it at once), and the line cards say when raiders' way in has moved. A new Almanac page explains how raiders pick their way.

The on-screen panels now sit beneath the game's own interface: windows, the colonist bar, letters, alerts and the inspect tabs draw over them, and your hover and clicks reach the game there. They stay visible behind open windows instead of disappearing ("hide them under big windows" is off now, still there as an option).

An Inventory panel shows what you have with the game's own icons, in four looks to try: classic, grouped by category, an icon grid and essentials only. Pin what matters, search, see the change since about this time yesterday, and click to jump to the stacks. The game's own resource list steps aside while it shows (a setting keeps both).

The health panel shows how each condition stands: tended and how well, how far a wound has healed and roughly when it will be gone, an illness's immunity race and whether it's being won. Right-click any alert in the Alerts panel to hide it there; the wishes the Council panel already shows are hidden by default.

The fungus meal is part fungus again, the rest any raw food, so the fungus lasts longer: a meal with some fungus in it is all a fungus diet asks. Stoves get a "cook 4 fungus meals" bill too, like the game's own.
Someone whose faith allows only one kind of food (a fungus or insect diet) no longer tires of the same meal: they have no choice to tire of.

The wedding wish no longer depends on the game choosing a day. Promise it and the council holds the wedding, the game's own ceremony, as soon as both are ready and the day is calm, trying again every few hours until it happens.
The wish says so: the game still marries an engaged couple on its own sooner or later, and a marriage spot gives the ceremony a place.

li.title: Alerts, health and work on screen

points.li: Your alerts in a panel you can move: the game's and every mod's, coloured by urgency, with the game's explanation on hover and its click to jump to them. The game's own list steps aside while the panel shows (a setting keeps both).

Health panel: only what will pass or needs seeing to (wounds, bleeding with the time left, anything untended, illnesses and whether they're winning), never scars, implants, chronic conditions, lost limbs or magical effects. Work and idle panel: what everyone is doing, who's idle and for how long, food, rest and recreation bars, and work nobody is set to do.

The panels always stay behind other windows. The game's own tooltip makes way for the hover card, which now puts long advice on its own line instead of cutting it, the mood trend's labels no longer overlap, and the "drag to move" tooltip is gone.

The fungus meal is now made from fungus and nothing else. When a colonist's faith requires fungus, Rimfolk makes a "Fungus diet" food policy once (fungus meals, raw fungus, insect jelly and insect meat only) and tells you who needs it. A policy that still allows simple meals or raw vegetables is what keeps such a colonist throwing up.
The small frictions between colonists (a borrowed thing not returned, a taken seat, a joke that fell flat) now say what they are and that they fade in a day or so, instead of pointing to the council.

World events that bring a family now bring one: a couple who share a name, sometimes with a child, and the dog or goat the text speaks of, tame and the colony's. Before, "the family" could be one person, and the dog never came. "The exiles" are always more than one, and no line assumes the colony already has a dog.

"The favorite" only comes when the same colonist has had a second wish granted since the other's own last one, within 30 days, while the other's request still waits. One wish granted is just good news.

On-screen panels: a mood board (every colonist's mood with their own break lines, where it's heading and the biggest thing dragging them down, most at risk first), a mood trend graph over 3 or 7 days, the colony's vitals (food days, medicine, power, the weather ahead, days since a raid, research) and the council at a glance (wishes, promises, questions, decrees, the next day or meeting, trust). Click through to the right place.

Every panel can be dragged, snaps to edges and other panels, and has its own options: rows and columns, sort, who's listed, compact or full, size and background. Toggle all of them with the button among the game's icons at the bottom right or a key, and find every option under Interface → On-screen panels.

Hover card: rest the mouse on a colonist on the map to see their mood and the two or three things that matter most right now, from bleeding and breaks to the biggest mood drag and what helps. Delay, modifier key, position and lines can all be set.

Badges on the colonist bar: a ring warms from amber to red as someone nears a break, and small badges mark someone about to leave, a wish waiting long, strain near breaking, wavering faith or a promise at risk. Hover for what and how much, click to go straight there. Each kind, the ring, size, corner and count can be set.

One shared ranking puts what matters most first everywhere: life and limb, then what's about to become a problem, then what's worth knowing; the biggest and most fixable first, and "and 3 more" rather than silently cutting a line.

The Mood tab opens compact: moods sorted into "You can fix", "Will pass", "Faith and who they are" and "Lifting", with chips for each group's total. Each mood is one line with its size and what helps ("Build a dining table") or how long it has left. Hover for the full explanation, click for its card with the advisor, council and Almanac buttons. "Details" brings back the old cards.
The game's own Needs tab gets one line above the moods with the same totals, so you can see how much is in your hands and how much will pass. Click it to open the Mood tab.
Every mood hint now has a short action, and the council's Moods page sorts the colony's moods the same way.

li.title: Social and Culture in the colonist's tabs

points.li: Rimfolk now sits in the game's own Social tab: a column beside the relations list with a colonist's bonds, groups and role, what people say about them, shared memories and in-jokes, recent talks and the secrets the colony knows. Hovering someone in the list adds a line on what is between the two of them. The "Rimfolk in the Social tab" setting turns it off.

A new Culture tab next to Social: faith with a certainty bar and any role, the views they hold, how they feel about the colony's ways, what they think of each decree in force, and where they come from.
The Story tab is lighter and keeps who they are and what they've lived through. The council's People page still shows everything.

People → Faiths (with Ideology): every faith in the colony on one page. It shows who believes what and how firmly, which faiths have no leader or moral guide here, what each faith asks that is weighing on someone right now, and who could sway whom. Each faith's card can call an evening of faith or name it the colony's faith, and the page explains the game's own tools.

Talks about faith matter: a devout, well-liked colonist who comes out of a friendly talk well sways someone of another faith a little. The open-minded and friends are swayed more, the proud less. An argument makes both dig in, two of one faith steady each other, and a faith that dislikes preaching takes it badly.

Evenings of faith: the council can call one from the faiths page or the calendar, or say yes when the devout ask. The faith's moral guide or most devout believer speaks, at its altar if one stands. Others choose whether to come, and a good evening can sway them and lifts those who came.
A wavering colonist may ask to spend an evening with a devout believer of another faith, to learn about it. Granted, the two sit together, and it moves them.

When the colony's faiths are at odds, the council decides: share the altar, give each faith its own corner, or name one faith the colony's. Each answer costs trust or certainty somewhere, and plays out on the map.

New decree, one faith for the colony: you name the faith. The wavering are drawn to it, its believers speak of it more often and meetings open with a word from it, while everyone else trusts the council a little less until it's lifted.

Crises of faith: losing someone for all the rites, being saved by someone of another faith, a faith's demands carried too long, or a brush with death can shake a colonist's faith for real. It shows as a turning point on their character page and in their journal.

Every conversion is the game's own: someone takes a new faith when their certainty runs out, and Rimfolk tells you who brought them round. The advisor speaks up when the colony is badly split. Two Almanac pages, "faith in the colony" and "faith and the council", explain it, and the "Faith in the colony" setting turns it all off.

Hard times: as a colonist nears breaking, Rimfolk's own small letdowns (a joke that fell flat, being talked about, a sticking door) weigh less, down to half at their break line, and its everyday pressures down to three quarters. It eases back as they recover. Low spirits no longer double the nightmares (sweet dreams still come rarely).

On the normal setting, everyday pressures and the colony's small frictions press at 85% of their old strength. The same work starts to wear after 4 days instead of 3, and a passion for the work takes it a step lighter.
Good moods add up a little faster: the third, fourth and fifth on a colonist's mind count for 60%, 45% and 35%, and every one after that a quarter.
"The favorite" now only comes to someone who really has a request of their own still waiting. Before, it could come to anyone when a wish was granted.

li.title: Eating well is no rut, and lean saves

points.li: Fine and lavish meals no longer count towards "the same meal again". A colonist who eats a fine meal every day enjoys it, and doesn't sour on it. Simple meals, pemmican and the like still count, and a varied table is still rewarded.

Saves stay lean: everything Rimfolk keeps now has a limit, about 2 MB after five years in a large colony. Curfews no longer keep notes on people the game has forgotten, and a removed map is no longer held on to for the defense line shown on it.

li.title: People with a character of their own

points.li: Every colonist has a character on eight sides (warmth, nerve, temper, humour, trust, pride, openness, outlook). Traits, the Social skill and age set where they start, and life marks them, with 48 kinds of mark: a raid held or a nerve broken, a friend lost, being nursed through an illness, a craft mastered, a hungry season. The Story tab opens with it: eight bars, and what shaped them, with dates.

Character shows in how they speak, in talk, gossip and the journal alike: a hothead snaps, a joker jokes, the cold are curt, the gloomy see the worst. It shows in what they do too: the warm have more warm moments, the hot-tempered more frictions, and the trusting confide their secrets sooner.

Conversations: two colonists who are together now and then really talk, a short exchange over their heads, taking turns. They talk about the last raid, the council, the food, the newcomer, faith and 14 more topics, and what comes up follows the news. Everyone holds a view on each topic, which moves slowly with what happens and with who talks them round, so a talk ends in agreement, a friendly debate, a heated argument, teasing or comfort.

Pairs keep shared memories: fighting side by side (only those who really stood together), a funeral, a feast, a caravan, a quarrel made up. Small mishaps become in-jokes once everyone's fine, funny for a while and then worn thin.

Groups grow out of something real (friendship, the same work, a fight, the night hours, faith, where they came from) and keep their name: the hunters, the night shift, Hector's lot. Each has roles, ways and habits, takes newcomers in or closes ranks, falls out with other groups, and can split or merge. People → Bonds shows each one.

Reputation and gossip: colonists notice what the others do (31 kinds of deed), and the rest hear it in gossip. Who tells it colours it, and the listener believes it as far as their nature lets them. What the colony knows becomes a name (brave or a coward, kind or cruel, reliable or idle), and a name leans votes and opinions.

Traits can change, rarely, after a long stretch of the same kind of life. Raid after raid held can make someone steadfast, a year of graves a pessimist, many kindnesses kind, and a beaten addiction a teetotaler. A psychopath or a cannibal comes only from an extreme history, once in a colony's life each. A letter tells what led to the change, with dates.

All of it gives opinion and company, not mood. "Personalities and social life" and "Traits can change" in the settings turn it off, and a new Almanac page, "Social life: how it fits together", follows two colonists through a year.

li.title: No more freeze when the region stirs

points.li: The game no longer freezes and then crashes when a world event is chosen for the region. Looking for a spot for "a new town nearby", Rimfolk started a second search of the world map inside the first, which the game can't survive. A save that crashed this way loads and plays on.
"Plans gathering dust" is gone: plans marked out and not yet started never weigh on anyone. Frames left half-built for two days still do.
The region's first world event comes sooner, around days 20 to 35, and until one has come the World page says how rare they are instead of standing empty.

li.title: Answers that happen before they're told

points.li: An answer that sets something going on the map no longer tells its outcome the moment it's given. It says when it's planned ("The harvest dance is planned for this evening"), and the story is told once it has happened, with how it went (meals eaten, jobs done). If it falls through, you hear that instead.

Answers that describe something done now do it on the map in 38 more places: the thief is punished in front of everyone at supper, the doctor sits at the bedside with the last dose, the snow is shovelled, the bees are smoked out, and the tribute, the bounty, the envoy's price and medicine for sick neighbors are carried out to the gate by hand.

li.title: Building up a defense, and the land's year

points.li: Defense lines: pick a gap on Colony → Defenses and build it up step by step with the helper, from closing the gap and clearing the field of fire, through cover, traps and guns, to a killbox, a second layer of wall and a line to fall back to. Steps tick themselves off from what stands, the line's aim (a gate, a killbox, a turret line, an archers' wall) orders them, and "Plan this step" opens the plan already placed and turned for the line. The killbox step says whether it fits behind the gap, what has to be dug or taken down, or where it would fit instead.

The helper reviews each line: where raiders could walk round it ("the wall stops 4 cells short of the rock to the west", with a button to wall it off), who sees the gate and from how far, trees and chunks raiders would hide behind (cut and haul in one click), turret spacing, power and fuel, wood in the wall, and a rough strength against today's raids.

Lines learn from raids: who came through the gate, went round or broke through, and where colonists fell. The lesson brings the right step to the front, and a reminder comes once per raid if a line's gate is shut. Defense plans now dig into unexplored rock the way room plans do.

Four new defense plans for building a line up step by step: a sandbag or barricade line behind a gate, a second layer of wall, a small killbox for narrow gaps and bows, and a tunnel killbox for mountain bases. The killbox is deeper, with its shooters out of grenade reach and walls between turrets and shooters, and the turret nest shields its repairer.

Five new Almanac pages on defending: defense lines step by step, where a killbox fits, killbox mistakes, the field of fire (weapon reach by era, and darkness as 1.6 really has it) and keeping a defense up. "How a killbox works" is rewritten in real RimWorld terms.

Wishes follow the land's year: clothes for the coming season (warm, or cool on hot land), measured by what the colonist wears; a freezer in hot country; and on cold land a sauna, with Dubs Bad Hygiene or without, where people sit and talk on cold days. Fishing wishes work with Odyssey or Vanilla Fishing Expanded.

The planting day: when the fields open after a cold season, the council asks whether to sow together. Held, it's a sowing party and a word at the field's edge in the evening, and a crop sown in full is remembered as a good start. You can also put a planting day on the calendar yourself.

The animals: a favourite kind of animal (or Pokémon) to wish for, a pack animal of one's own, and bringing the herd home before winter or after a raid, each animal walked into the barn or pen on a rope.

li.title: Fungus meals and digging into the dark

points.li: With Ideology, a "cook fungus meal" bill at any stove makes simple meals that always have fungus in them, a kind of meal of their own, so one colonist's food policy can take only these while everyone else's leaves them out (Alpha Memes' fungus diet no longer makes them sick). A new Almanac page, "fungus meals", shows how to set it up.

Room plans reach into unexplored ground: the inside is marked for mining and dug out as the colonists get there, rock in the walls stays as the wall, and the rest of the room (walls on open ground, the door, furniture and floor) follows as the ground comes to light.

Colony → Defenses reads your map: the edges raiders come from, the narrow places on their way in, whether the home is walled in, and advice ranked by what matters now, with eleven defense plans you place like room plans. Fifteen new Almanac pages on defending the colony.

The advisor watches 62 kinds of thing: a mission running out, plague or famine in the region, a camp's question or an office left waiting, the low-tech winter, and rooms that could be better. Some advice takes the first step for you.

The colony's animals: the herdmaster's rounds, an animal of one's own to wish for, stories of an old companion or an orphan raised by hand, hard choices about the herd, and the lambing watch and shearing day as traditions. With PokéWorld, trainers spar and talk moves, and the council can set out to fill a Pokédex.

Four new scenarios: The Elders' Fire, What the Ship Carried, The Orphanage (Biotech) and The Land Grant. A colony can become known for its hospitality, its faith or the days it keeps, and people earn names from their years in a seat, the faith and the colony.

Health that follows what happened: a cough after the flu, swellings after the plague, a limp once a broken leg has healed, bad nights after a fight at home, and with the DLCs a pollution cough, unease after a horror and sickness aloft. The hospital earns a name of its own that eases its patients and draws the sick from the road; convalescence can follow hunger, cold or an illness nobody tended.
Nemeses in dreams, a story of the fear laid to rest once one is caught, and the day one first came back on the calendar; feelings now move with the camps and the region's troubles.

About 3,000 new lines where colonists repeated themselves most: everyday journals, wish reminders and thanks, personal touches, meeting talk, moments between colonists, dreams over breakfast, what colonists say aloud, walks, vigils and hunts, camps' requests, the newer decrees, and around the animals (a pet's mischief, the herd's habits, a Pokémon evolving). What two colonists say when one walks over to the other (a secret confided, a mentor's thanks, the physician's rounds, the marshal's word) now goes a dozen or more ways. The lines heard most come round about once a year or less.

This page, a CHANGELOG.md with the same list, and a letter when you load a save after an update (a new colony gets the welcome letter instead; the Interface page of the settings can turn it off). The council window now reopens on the page you last had open (a setting can make it open on This week instead).

li.title: The colony's year, the world beyond and people's lives

points.li: Conversations happen where people are: a colonist walks over before talking, and every line is spoken the same way, as a bubble or floating text.
Wishes, feasts and toasts respect each colonist's beliefs and diet.
The colony's year: new decrees and offices, calendar days, customs and council projects for a settled people.
The world beyond the walls: ten regional situations, eight new kinds of camp with requests of their own, missions of the road, and peoples who remember single colonists.
People's lives: personal stories of three, life goals that grow up with a child, more for the young and the old.
More answers play out on the map: work parties, walks, vigils, searches, errands and hunts (only safe game, and nothing someone else has claimed).
Wall lamps chosen by room size and hung on a real wall; mods round three (Outland, Medieval Total Rim, Alpha Genes and Memes); a lighter pass on the game.

The council window opens on This week: what waits on you, what's coming and how people are. Everyone is one sortable table of the colonists, and Dilemmas keeps every question and how each answer went.
41 setbacks: bad moods that come from what happens in play, each with a hint about what helps.
Promises kept: a granted wish can be taken back, and colonists notice.
Good moods are smaller and fewer; many small good moments now give something else (rest, recreation, a lesson, trust or a feeling).
Rimfolk's systems react to each other, and colonists say aloud how they feel, talk about the weather and keep small habits (a grave visited, the stars watched, a slow walk).
A balance pass from a simulated colony year, and your other mods in Rimfolk's newer systems.

li.title: The calendar, personal stories and answers that play out

points.li: The colony calendar: days that matter, kept each year.
Sixteen personal stories that unfold over seasons, and health stories: convalescence, sickbed visits, doctors' and midwives' records.
Answers play out on the map: when a council answer says people feast, light a fire, raise a toast or visit a grave, they do.
What the world's peoples remember of the colony, and events that follow from it.
A settings window with pages, search and presets; one evening letter for the day's smaller news; room themes and advice when the colony outgrows a room.
The breadth round: more secrets, vendettas, offices, customs, names, scenarios and feelings, and 1,830 more lines for the thinnest pools.
A more readable Almanac, with tables and a text size.

li.title: RimWorld 1.7, ailments, and more to say

points.li: Rimfolk runs on RimWorld 1.7 as well as 1.6, with one file for both.
Everyday ailments (colds, strained backs, sunburn) and a rare tier of serious illnesses.
Visual and sound touches from the game's own effects: sky tints, fireflies, camp smoke, celebrations.
About 1,700 new lines, and a memory that keeps a line from coming round again too soon.
Good times turn ordinary: good memories fade sooner, and standards rise to cover the game's comforts.
Room plans: 28 room types and 108 layouts. A welcome letter, a "Start here" page and a self-check.
More wishes, council projects, life goals, dilemmas, encounters, decrees and quirks, and a soft integration for PokéWorld.

li.title: Meetings that happen, and rooms of every size

points.li: Council meetings are announced, colonists are called in, and those who miss one miss it for a reason.
Rewards are earned instead of handed out, and everyday pressures push back on a colony that has it easy.
Rooms: sizes and styles, eighteen new rooms, your own saved rooms, and how much of each material you have in the build menu.
Everyday journal entries drawn from what is on a colonist's mind.
Everyday frictions with each other and with the home itself: sticking doors, leaks, smoke and clutter.
Feelings and strain: a layer under mood that builds through hard times and eases with rest, friends and quiet.
Camps on the colony's map, region-wide situations, storyteller events, story chains and missions.
Integrations with home-life and people mods: Dubs Bad Hygiene, Hospitality, Vanilla Cooking and Brewing, Outposts, RimHUD, A RimWorld of Magic and more.
Every Almanac page rewritten in a shape of its own, and the text read through for a plainer voice.
Encounters with wildlife, visitors, traders, prisoners and fallen enemies; nemeses who come back, and pets with moments of their own.
27 new wishes, 72 in all, and 38 moments between colonists.
The colony's character: what the council keeps choosing shapes who the colony is.
A Mood tab for each colonist, a Moods page for the colony, and half and quarter speed for unhurried planning.
World events, six scenarios, Almanac pages for many popular mods, and install or update with a double-click.
The first versions: an advisor, wishes and the council's answers, meetings with speeches and votes, ambitions, the room planner and the Almanac.
Decrees, dilemmas, traditions, offices and yearly elections.
Journals, yearly annals, anniversaries and names earned by deeds.
Friendships, rivalries and mentors, dreams and omens, life goals, secrets, vendettas, eulogies, quirks and heirlooms, all on a Story tab for each colonist.
